front: What are the FSF’s four essential freedoms, by number?
back: 0: run the program for any purpose. 1: study and change it. 2: share copies. 3: share your changed versions.

front: Which two of the four freedoms need access to the source code?
back: Freedom 1 (study and change the program) and freedom 3 (share your changed versions).

front: Does "free software" mean it costs nothing?
back: No. "Free" means freedom, not price. Free software can be sold, and software that costs nothing can still be proprietary.

front: Who started the Free Software Foundation (FSF), and around which project?
back: Richard Stallman, around the GNU project. For the FSF, users’ freedom is an ethical matter.

front: What is the Open Source Initiative (OSI), and what does it maintain?
back: The OSI, founded in the late 1990s, makes a practical case that open development gives better software. It maintains the Open Source Definition with ten criteria and approves open source licences.

front: How do the Free Software and Open Source movements differ, and do they usually accept different programs?
back: They differ in emphasis (ethics versus practical benefits), not mostly in programs. Nearly every free software licence is also an open source licence, and the other way round.

front: What do FOSS and FLOSS stand for?
back: FOSS is free and open source software; FLOSS is free/libre and open source software. "Libre" stresses "free" as in freedom, not price.

front: What is the difference between copyleft and permissive licences?
back: Copyleft requires anyone who passes the software on to keep the same freedoms and licence. A permissive licence puts few conditions on reuse and even lets others make their changes proprietary.

front: Which licence covers the Linux kernel, and is it copyleft or permissive?
back: The GPL (GNU General Public License), the best-known copyleft licence. Many GNU tools use it too.

front: What are the LGPL and the AGPL?
back: Both are copyleft variants. The LGPL is a weaker version made for libraries. The AGPL extends copyleft to programs people only use over a network.

front: What does a BSD licence mostly require?
back: Keeping the copyright notice (and the licence text), and not using the authors’ names to promote your product. It is permissive, so a company may sell improved code without releasing it.

front: What do the Creative Commons elements BY, SA, NC and ND mean?
back: BY: credit the creator (attribution). SA: share adaptations under the same terms. NC: non-commercial use only. ND: no derivatives, copy and share but don’t change.

front: Jonas publishes sprites under CC BY-SA. What may others do with them?
back: Reuse and remix them, including commercially, if they credit Jonas and share their remixes under the same terms.

front: Which Creative Commons licence is the most open, which the most restrictive, and what is CC0?
back: CC BY is the most open and CC BY-NC-ND the most restrictive. CC0 gives up as many rights as the law allows, so anyone can use the work without conditions.

front: Are Creative Commons licences meant for software?
back: No. They are for content such as art, music, photos and manuals. For code, use a software licence.

front: What is proprietary software?
back: Software whose owner decides what you may do with it, typically a binary with a restrictive licence and no source code. It can be free of charge, so price is not the test; the freedoms are.

front: What is digital autonomy?
back: The ability of a person or organisation to decide for themselves which software they run, where their data is stored and whether they can leave a supplier.

front: What is digital sovereignty, and how is it related to digital autonomy?
back: The same idea at the level of a country, public body or company: control over their own digital infrastructure, data and rules. Open licences give control and the ability to leave.

front: What is vendor lock-in?
back: Dependence on one supplier’s proprietary product, so you can’t easily inspect, fix or switch away from it. Open source lets you read, change and move your software.

front: Ada chose a self-hosted code forge over a proprietary hosting service. Which idea backs this argument?
back: Digital autonomy: the studio controls its source code and can move it without asking anyone.

front: Name three ways open source companies earn money.
back: Support and subscriptions (Red Hat, SUSE), services and consulting, hosting as a service. Also dual licensing, open core, donations and selling hardware.

front: What is the difference between dual licensing and open core?
back: Dual licensing sells the same code under a free licence and a paid commercial one. Open core keeps the core free and sells extra features under a proprietary licence.

front: TuxPixel wants other small studios to use its engine even in commercial games. Which kind of licence fits?
back: A permissive one. A copyleft licence would require others to share their changes too.

front: Where does Debian keep copies of the common licences, and which one starts with "GNU GENERAL PUBLIC LICENSE Version 3"?
back: In `/usr/share/common-licenses/`. The file `GPL-3` there is the GPL version 3.

front: Which organisation is behind the "four essential freedoms" and which behind the "Open Source Definition"?
back: The Free Software Foundation (FSF) wrote the four freedoms. The Open Source Initiative (OSI) maintains the Open Source Definition.

front: Mira reads that a licence is "OSI approved". What does that tell her?
back: It counts as an open source licence: the Open Source Initiative checked it against the ten criteria of the Open Source Definition.

front: What does the 2-clause BSD licence ask?
back: Keep the copyright notice and the disclaimer. It is permissive. FreeBSD, NetBSD and OpenBSD are BSD operating systems.

front: What is the GNU FDL?
back: The GNU Free Documentation License: copyleft for manuals and other documentation.

front: What is a fork?
back: A copy of a project’s source code that is developed separately, such as LibreOffice from OpenOffice.org.
